source: Perez et al. (2025, ICLR) When LLMs play the telephone game: cultural attractors as conceptual tools to evaluate LLMs in multi-turn settings
finding: Bartlett-style transmission chains with LLMs. Each model rewrites the previous model's text. Text properties drift toward an attractor. The less constrained the instruction, the stronger the pull.
numbers: 6 models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Llama3-8B and 70B, Mistral-7B, Mixtral-8x7B), 3 tasks (Rephrase, Take inspiration, Continue), 20 initial texts x 5 seeds = 100 chains per cell, 50 generations. Attractor strength: Continue > Take inspiration > Rephrase (Bayesian 95% CIs). KS tests vs generation 1 show p falling with generations, more so for open tasks.
quote: more open-ended instructions lead to stronger attraction effects compared to more constrained tasks
limits: Measures toxicity, positivity, difficulty and length, not factual content. No human control chain. Strength is a fitted linear-regression slope.
agent_relevance: Iterating an LLM over its own output (summaries of summaries, memory rewrites) pulls text to model-specific defaults. Constrain rewrite steps and keep the original text. Never re-summarise a summary.

source: Perez et al. (2025, ICLR) When LLMs play the telephone game: cultural attractors as conceptual tools to evaluate LLMs in multi-turn settings
finding: Attractor strength and position depend on model, temperature and fine-tuning. Bigger or newer models pulled less.
numbers: Llama3-70B and GPT-4o-mini had significantly weaker attractors than GPT-3.5, Llama3-8B and Mixtral-8x7B. Higher temperature raised attractor strength only in constrained tasks (Rephrase, Take inspiration), not in Continue. Instruct vs Base: attractor for length lower and for difficulty higher; toxicity and positivity attractors not clearly shifted. Robust to 100 initial texts and to prompt rephrasing.
limits: Only these model versions (2024). Temperature result is described by the authors as an interpretation.
agent_relevance: The size of the schema-like pull is a model property we can measure. Test our own backbone with a short chain before trusting multi-step memory.

source: Perez et al. (2025, ICLR) When LLMs play the telephone game: cultural attractors as conceptual tools to evaluate LLMs in multi-turn settings
finding: Different properties converge differently. Toxicity collapses to near 0 fast. Positivity ends bimodal for Llama3. Length goes down for GPT-3.5 and Llama3-8B but up for Mixtral and GPT-4o-mini.
numbers: Toxicity strongest attractor of the four properties (significant against positivity, difficulty, length). Positivity attractor position significantly lower for Llama3-8B than for GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini, Mistral-7B, Mixtral. Take inspiration and Continue gave higher positivity than Rephrase.
limits: Property-level, not content-level, so it does not show which facts are dropped.
agent_relevance: Drift is not neutral: iterated rewrites also add positivity or cut length depending on model. Log length and tone across scaffold steps as a drift alarm.

source: Acerbi and Stubbersfield (2023) Large language models show human-like content biases in transmission chain experiments
finding: ChatGPT-3 repeated summarising reproduced the human biases from 5 earlier transmission-chain studies, including keeping stereotype-consistent details over stereotype-inconsistent ones.
numbers: 5 preregistered experiments, 3 summarising iterations, 5 replications each, mixed models. Stereotype-consistent retained more (beta=0.058, P<0.01). Negative over positive (beta=0.117); ambiguity resolved negatively (beta=0.183); social over non-social (beta=0.321); threat over negative/neutral (beta=0.523); biological counterintuitive/social/negative (beta=0.076). All P<0.001 except as noted.
quote: stereotype-consistent information was reproduced more than stereotype-inconsistent information through the chain
limits: One model (ChatGPT-3), short chains (3 steps), betas are mixed-model coefficients on proportion retained, not standardised effects. Authors say bias is not inherently bad.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an LLM keeps schema-consistent content and drops schema-inconsistent content when it compresses text. A summariser step in our scaffold can silently delete the surprising fact that matters.

source: Meylan, Nair and Griffiths (2021) Evaluating models of robust word recognition with serial reproduction
finding: Serial reproduction converges on listeners' priors. Language models that use phrase structure best predict the changes people make over chains.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; the paper compares several probabilistic language models against chains of utterances. Convergence to the stationary distribution needs enough iterations. Model ranking numbers not extracted.
limits: Short sentence level, spoken input; not story recall.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal reading of Bartlett: each retelling samples from the prior, so a language model prior can be tested as the schema. Link to the transmission-chain LLM work.

source: Hippocampo-neocortical interaction as compressive retrieval-augmented generation (2026, PMC13447824)
finding: A model stores a compressed gist plus surprising details and rebuilds the story with an LLM. This gives the same kinds of schema intrusions as Bartlett's subjects, and consolidating the rebuilt story makes it worse.
numbers: 500 ROC Stories encoded: gist-only, gist+1 detail, gist+3 details, full text and 'imagine from background knowledge' compared on tokens stored vs cosine similarity to original; gist+details strikes the balance. Mistral-7B fine-tuned on Wikipedia categories (1000 articles each; Politics, Health, Universe, Sport, Nature) then on the War of the Ghosts: intrusions match the training topic (e.g. football for Sport). More intrusions at higher temperature; distortion occurs even at greedy decoding. Consolidated recall more distorted than encoded recall.
quote: consolidation of a compressed memory is an 'approximation of an approximation'
limits: Simulation, not a human replication. Similarity is measured by embedding cosine (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), not by human scoring. Model is a theory demonstration.
agent_relevance: Shows that an LLM-based memory (compress then regenerate) will be pulled toward its own priors. Store verbatim surprising details and regenerate only the rest; do not reuse regenerated memories as new inputs.

source: Hippocampo-neocortical interaction as compressive retrieval-augmented generation (2026, PMC13447824)
finding: Same paper re-uses the human Bergman and Roediger replication data: fraction of recalled propositions with major distortions rises with delay. Also models event extension and contraction (Raykov et al.).
numbers: Human data reproduced from Bergman and Roediger (1999) in Fig 5b; exact proportions not stated in text, so not recorded here. Event extension: incomplete videos extended in memory, updated videos shortened.
limits: Secondary citation of the replication; check the original for figures.
agent_relevance: Time and repeated retrieval increase schema-driven distortion. Prefer fresh retrieval from source over retrieval from earlier summaries.

source: Sweegers et al. (2015) Mental schemas hamper memory storage of goal-irrelevant information
finding: A schema that already solves the task makes people encode less of the item. Schema-congruent faces were remembered worse than schema-incongruent ones, the opposite of the usual congruency benefit.
numbers: N=48 (F(1,47)). Learning phase: schema-congruent face-home matches 34.65/36 (SD 1.44) vs incongruent 28.21 (SD 6.86), Z=-5.74, p<.001. Recognition d': congruent 1.31 vs incongruent 1.67; global 1.88 vs 2.31, detailed 0.74 vs 1.03 (Z=-4.58, Z=-3.92, both p<.001). Parietal old/new ERP smaller for congruent items.
quote: schema-congruency induced substantial impairments in item memory and even larger ones in context memory
limits: Artificial rule-based schema learned the day before, one lab, faces and homes. Goal made item detail redundant. Not a naturalistic schema.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: when a schema suffices for the task, detail is not stored. An agent that leans on a template will log less of the specifics. Force verbatim capture of inputs before applying a schema.

source: Cockcroft, Berens, Gaskell and Horner (2022) Schematic information influences memory and generalisation behaviour for schema-relevant and -irrelevant information (Cognition; OSF preprint)
finding: Four preregistered experiments (two replication pairs): a clustered pattern lets people extract a schema, and it changes where they put new words. The memory benefit was small and unstable.
numbers: Exp 1 final N=63; Exp 2 N=75 (24h delay); Exp 3 N=63 (replicates Exp 1); Exp 4 replicates Exp 2. Memory: clustered > non-clustered, t(124)=1.99, p=.049, d=0.35, BF01=0.87 (inconclusive) in Exp 1; Exp 2 no difference, t(148)=0.67, p=.502, d=0.11, BF01=4.63. Generalisation to new words fit the imposed distribution better for clustered: Exp 1 d=0.76, BF01=0.001; Exp 2 d=0.54, BF01=0.04. No change after the delay, d=0.19, BF01=3.20.
quote: participants placed novel words in the clustered category in similar locations to the old clustered items
limits: Word-location task with circular precision measure, psychology undergraduates. Schema is the imposed pattern.
agent_relevance: Replicated part: a learned pattern drives guessing for unseen items (schema as prior). Unreplicated part: memory benefit. Schema-irrelevant controls are contaminated too, so control tests must be built carefully.

source: Cockcroft, Berens, Gaskell and Horner (2022) Schematic information influences memory and generalisation behaviour for schema-relevant and -irrelevant information (Cognition; OSF preprint)
finding: Schema effect leaks into 'schema-irrelevant' items: people avoided placing non-clustered items near the clustered pattern.
numbers: Avoidance effect present in Experiment 1 and no longer present in Experiment 2 (24h delay), per the paper's discussion. Uniformity of non-clustered responses did not differ from clustered: t(124)=0.08, p=.933, d=0.02, BF01=5.24.
limits: Avoidance effect unstable across experiments. Exploratory reading.
agent_relevance: A template can bias even the items it does not cover. Keep control cases out of the context that holds the schema.

source: Xu, Hemmer and Zhang (2023) Towards a generalized Bayesian model of reconstructive memory (PsyArXiv)
finding: Rival models: the Category Adjustment Model (Huttenlocher 2000) predicts atypical items are pulled more toward the category centre. Newer data show typical items are pulled more. The generalised CAM fits both.
numbers: Tompary and Thompson-Schill (2021) and Zeng et al. (2021) showed the atypicality effect: typical members more biased to category centre than atypical ones; no difference when items were not arranged by category (scrambled control). g-CAM reproduces the ordering; simulated average bias was slightly negative where the human bias was positive.
quote: reconstructive memory for atypical category examples is influenced by the category center less than that of typical category examples
limits: Simulation paper, no new human data. Discrepancy in bias sign blamed on grid layout.
agent_relevance: Prior-knowledge pull is not constant: it is stronger when the item looks typical of the schema. A schema-based filter will distort typical-looking inputs most, which are the ones we least check.

source: Tompary and Thompson-Schill (2021) Semantic influences on episodic memory distortions (OSF preprint u754s)
finding: Four experiments. Location memory was more accurate for images in category-consistent places. When images were in inconsistent places, typical members were pulled toward their category more than atypical ones.
numbers: Effects replicated across three experiments; disappeared when images were not arranged by category; stronger than effects from visual-similarity arrangement. Per-experiment N not extracted.
quote: retrieval of typical category members was more biased towards other category members relative to atypical ones
limits: Spatial-memory paradigm with images; numbers read only from the abstract and the g-CAM summary.
agent_relevance: Use as the clean replicated finding for 'typicality moderates schema distortion'.

source: Conceptual vs perceptual features and memory distortion (OSF preprint swy32, 2025)
finding: When prior knowledge has conceptual and perceptual cues, conceptual cues win. Alone, each pulls memory about equally.
numbers: In isolation conceptual and perceptual clusters produced distortions of equivalent magnitude; when competing, images were biased mainly to the conceptual cluster. Persisted when the encoding task prioritised perceptual features. Numeric values not recorded.
quote: conceptual features play a privileged role in the organization of new long-term memories regardless of encoding demands
limits: Image-location task, preprint, authors not extracted.
agent_relevance: Meaning-level schemas dominate surface cues, so label-level cues will hijack recall more than format cues.

source: Curtis, Denneen, Wimber and Horner (2026) Memory benefits for schematically incongruent sequences depend on the type of violation (OSF preprint 56kqr)
finding: Both congruent and incongruent sequences were remembered better than schema-unrelated ones. The incongruent benefit appeared only for content violations, not for order violations, even though both produced prediction error.
numbers: 4 experiments, 193 university students total (Exp 4 final N=42). Planned power: N=45 for at least 80% power for d=0.28 congruent effect and d=0.12 incongruent effect.
quote: incongruent benefits are not the inevitable consequence of prediction error at encoding
limits: Four-item artificial sequences. Authors flag naturalistic temporal order as untested.
agent_relevance: Surprise helps memory only for some kinds of violation. A schema that is wrong about order may go undetected and unremembered.

source: Nguyen, McRae and Zacks (2026) How schemas shape memory for everyday activities: the roles of surprise and prediction uncertainty (OSF preprint dc9tw)
finding: Experiment designed to discriminate SLIMM (U-shape for gist) from schema-copy-plus-tag (monotonic). Gist memory rose with surprise; the schema-consistent end did not get a boost. Schema-consistent information was not forgotten more slowly over 24 hours.
numbers: Study 1a N=67 (70 recruited, 3 excluded), 30 minute test; Study 1b: 46 of those 67 returned at 24 h; Study 2 N=62. Gist but not detail memory better for more surprising events. Surprise driven by contextual appropriateness, more strongly when the violation hits goal-relevant actions. Gist better for high-uncertainty moments (Study 3).
quote: gist memory is enhanced when events are surprising or uncertain
limits: Written narratives of everyday activities, English speakers, online. Study 3 reanalyses Study 1a data.
agent_relevance: Supports 'doubt on a signal' (G1): a surprise signal buys extra processing. The signal for an LLM would be a check failure or a low-probability event, not the schema match.

source: Gustarova and Chromy (2026) A deer in the elevator: the effect of information congruency on immediate recall and delayed recognition (OSF preprint 5dsvq)
finding: Four self-paced reading experiments in Czech. Congruent locations recalled better right after reading, but the advantage was gone at delayed recognition.
numbers: Experiment 1 final N=195; a later experiment N=183. Immediate recall favoured congruent locations across experiments; delayed word recognition showed no reliable congruency advantage.
quote: incongruent information must pass a higher threshold to be encoded, but once it is successfully encoded, it is no longer disadvantaged
limits: Sentence-level congruency in Czech, reading-time paradigm. Not a replication of Brewer and Treyens. Author names partly not extracted.
agent_relevance: Congruency advantage is an encoding-time threshold effect: incongruent items need more to get in, but once in they last. Mismatches should be flagged at read time.

source: Mubarak and Fukuda (2026) The price of prediction: robust false memories in naturalistic contexts (OSF preprint acshn)
finding: Making a prediction creates a false memory of the predicted event, even when the video then shows a different outcome. This held with instructions to remember the real outcome, and grew without instructions.
numbers: Exp 1a N=71: no-feedback false memory M=0.153, d=1.080; after direct rebuttal M=0.035, d=0.519, still above zero; reduction vs no-feedback d=0.820. Exp 1b N=67, no instruction: no-feedback M=0.221 (d=1.061), rebuttal M=0.060 (d=0.338). No-feedback larger in 1b than 1a, M=0.226 vs 0.157, t(140)=2.149, d=0.361. Effect survived a 24h delay (Exp 2a N=66, 2b N=67) and was stronger without feedback as true memories faded.
quote: merely generating a prediction is sufficient to induce a false memory of the predicted event
limits: Short first-person videos, undergraduates, preprint. Effect is a few percent of trials after rebuttal.
agent_relevance: Strong analogue: an LLM that commits to a hypothesis keeps it in memory even after contrary output. Rebuttal cut the effect by about 77% here (0.153 to 0.035) but did not remove it. Keep the guess out of the record that is later read as fact.

source: Mubarak, Bulatova, Halabisaz, Yuan and Fukuda (2026) Prediction-based false memories are resistant to violation magnitude and temporal decay (OSF preprint g8peq)
finding: Prediction-based false memory survived large violations, survived decoupling from action, survived predicting the schema-inconsistent colour, and survived an overnight delay.
numbers: Four experiments, N=68, 70, 66, 65. Exp 3 (predict the most surprising colour): no-feedback colour-memory above baseline, d=1.367; schema-consistent predictions gave larger false memory than inconsistent, d=0.610; peak persisted when prediction contradicted prior schema, d=0.567 vs confirmation. Violation vs no feedback d>0.259 (p near .07).
quote: Schema consistency augments both true and false memory
limits: Colour-wheel task with silhouettes; effect less precise for schema-inconsistent guesses (larger arc size, d=0.367).
agent_relevance: Schema consistency adds to both true and false memory. Counter to the idea that surprising guesses are safe from fixation.

source: Prior knowledge and the recall of single events and instances of repeated events: a registered report (OSF preprint 7tg4p, 2025)
finding: Registered report. High prior knowledge gave more correct details and higher understanding. Single events were recalled better than the last instance of a repeated event, and this did not depend on prior knowledge.
numbers: Exp 1 validated 3 stimulus sets. Exp 2 replicated the single-vs-repeated recall deficit across prior-knowledge conditions, contrary to the authors' expectation. First instance of repeated event vs single event: small, nonsignificant difference.
limits: Authors not recorded. Effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Repeated similar episodes blur into one schema, losing instance detail, even for experts. Keep per-case logs apart from the general pattern.

source: Predicting memory distortions in hundreds of verbal recalls (OSF preprint sfqea, LLM annotation)
finding: GPT-4o in-context labelled false memories in 229 people's spoken recalls of 4 narratives. Similarity to prototypical narrative text predicts factual conflicts; surprise predicts confabulations.
numbers: N=229 participants (mean age 25.03). Event recalled by 48.6% [45.1, 52.1]. False memory rate among recalled events 27.4% [25.5, 29.4], factual conflicts 22.4%, confabulations 7.7%. One SD more semantic centrality raised recall odds 12% (OR=1.12 [1.05, 1.18]). Similarity to narrative corpus gave more factual conflicts (beta=0.15, p<0.001, OR=1.16); contextual surprisal gave more confabulations (beta=0.15, p=0.005, OR=1.16). Replicated with USE and Pythia embeddings.
limits: LLM labels, not a human gold standard; effects small (OR 1.16). Corpus similarity measured by MPNet embeddings against NarrativeXL.
agent_relevance: Schema pull and surprise are separate error drivers. Different guards: grounded check for typical-looking content, an extra check for surprising content.

source: Predicting memory distortions in hundreds of verbal recalls (OSF preprint sfqea, LLM annotation)
finding: Validation of LLM detection of memory errors against humans. Accurate-vs-inaccurate labelling reached near-perfect agreement with trained raters, but error-type labelling stayed weak.
numbers: Run-to-run agreement of the pipeline 95.3% (false memory), 97.3% (factual conflict), 92.0% (confabulation). Online raters, open-ended task: inter-human 0.60 (29 raters, 60 sentences). Forced-choice version with 70 online participants raised agreement. Expert raters: inter-subject 0.78; human-AI Cohen's kappa 0.87 for accurate vs inaccurate; error type kappa 0.27 (fair), human-AI 0.63 vs inter-subject.
limits: Expert checks used one narrative (Pieman), 30 and 49 sentences. Single model GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: LLM judges can detect distortions against a source text when the source is shown, which supports code-checked grounding but not self-judged type labelling.

source: Bergman and Roediger (1999) Can Bartlett's repeated reproduction experiments be replicated? Memory and Cognition 27:937-947
finding: Close replication: after 15 min, 1 week and 6 months, people forgot, added rationalisation and distortion, and imported new propositions. Earlier partial replications had failed.
numbers: Abstract page only: tests at 15 min, 1 week, and a 6-month follow-up on as many subjects as could be obtained; share of distorted material rose with delay. Sample sizes and proportions not read (full text paywalled; cited via PMC13447824).
quote: Bartlett's repeated reproduction results can be replicated
limits: Full text not opened. Bartlett's 'increasing errors in the same people' claim is what was replicated.
agent_relevance: The classic result holds, but this is one lab. Treat time-delay distortion as likely but its size as unknown.

source: Wynn and Logie (1998) The veracity of long-term memory: did Bartlett get it right? Applied Cognitive Psychology 12:1-20
finding: Failure to support: students repeatedly recounted real events from their first university weeks and showed little change and few errors over time. Authors tied it to limits on constructive processing.
numbers: Secondary report only (a Chinese journal review seen in a search snippet). No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened. Different material (self-experienced events, not a foreign folktale), so not a direct replication; reviewer says events may be unusually memorable.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: meaningful, well-known events resist schema drift in repeated retelling. Distortion is a function of material strangeness.

source: Gauld and Stephenson (1967) Some experiments relating to Bartlett's theory of remembering, British Journal of Psychology 58
finding: Recalled from background knowledge, NOT verified: instructions stressing accuracy reduced apparent distortions in War of the Ghosts recall, suggesting some errors were guesses under loose instructions.
numbers: No numbers verified. Citation metadata only (Crossref, 72 citations).
limits: Not opened. The claim is from memory and must be checked before use.
agent_relevance: If true, accuracy instructions and source-check prompts reduce schema-filled errors. Worth testing on the LLM: strict-recall vs free prompt.

source: Brewer and Treyens (1981) Role of schemata in memory for places, Cognitive Psychology 13
finding: Founding office-room study: people recall and recognise schema-consistent objects they never saw. Counts were not read this session.
numbers: Crossref metadata only (562 citations). No participant counts or intrusion rates verified.
limits: Not opened. Do not quote numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for 'schema fills gaps with expected items'.

source: Lampinen, Copeland and Neuschatz (2001) Recollections of things schematic: room schemas revisited, JEP:LMC 27:1211
finding: Replication and extension of Brewer and Treyens room-schema work; metadata shows it exists with 75 citations. Results not read.
numbers: Crossref metadata only.
limits: Not opened. Findings must be extracted before use.
agent_relevance: Candidate key replication to open next.

source: Rojahn and Pettigrew (1992) Memory for schema-relevant information: a meta-analytic resolution, Br J Soc Psychol 31
finding: A meta-analysis aimed at settling whether schema-incongruent or schema-congruent information is remembered better; existence and 131 citations confirmed, effect sizes not.
numbers: Crossref metadata only. No effect sizes recorded.
limits: Not opened. Social-cognition sample (person memory), so may not transfer. Pair with Stangor and McMillan (1992), not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Meta-analytic anchor for the 'which wins' question. Open this next.

source: Alba and Hasher (1983) Is memory schematic? Psychological Bulletin 93:203-231
finding: Classic critique (from background knowledge, not verified): schema theories bundle selection, abstraction, interpretation, integration and reconstruction, and the evidence for several is weak.
numbers: Crossref metadata only (806 citations). No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Claim list is from memory.
agent_relevance: Reminder that 'schema' is a bundle of processes, so test each separately in the agent.

source: Tuckey and Brewer (2003) How schemas affect eyewitness memory over repeated retrieval attempts, Applied Cognitive Psychology 17
finding: Eyewitness study of how schemas affect memory over repeated retrieval; existence confirmed, findings not read.
numbers: Crossref metadata only (34 citations).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Open next for retrieval-repetition effects (does repeated recall strengthen schema errors).

source: Ghosh and Gilboa (2014) What is a memory schema? Neuropsychologia 53
finding: Defines a memory schema by four necessary features: associative network, basis on multiple episodes, lack of unit detail, adaptability. Four extra features: chronological, hierarchical, cross-connected, embedded response options.
numbers: Abstract read through Europe PMC record; 277 citations.
limits: Full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable definition of 'schema' for our scaffold; our templates lack 'adaptability' unless revised from failures (G2).

source: Raykov et al. (2026) Predictions and declarative memory encoding: two fMRI paradigms provide slim pickings for SLIMM, Phil Trans R Soc B
finding: Partial failed replication of SLIMM. Both studies reproduced the U-shape between expectancy and memory, but neither found the predicted interaction in hippocampus or medial prefrontal cortex.
numbers: Abstract read through Europe PMC record: two fMRI paradigms (object locations in scenes; idiom completions). Sample sizes not read.
limits: Full text not opened.
agent_relevance: The behavioural U-shape is more robust than the proposed mechanism. Do not build the agent on SLIMM details.

source: Kleider, Pezdek, Goldinger and Kirk (2008) Schema-driven source misattribution errors: remembering the expected from a witnessed event, Applied Cognitive Psychology
finding: Schema-driven source misattribution: people remember expected things as part of an event. Detail not read.
numbers: Crossref metadata only (80 citations); online date 2007-2008.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate source for the source-monitoring side of schema errors.

source: Hemmer and Steyvers (2009) A Bayesian account of reconstructive memory, Topics in Cognitive Science 1
finding: Extends the category-adjustment model to several levels of prior knowledge; recall is biased toward category and item priors, with weights set by uncertainty.
numbers: Europe PMC record exists; full text blocked (403). Claim is as described in the g-CAM paper (b11), not verified in the original.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Rational account: more uncertain memory leans harder on the schema. Rule for an agent: lean on templates only when evidence is weak.
